How many real sync calls does that actually end up making?
Exactly a thousand.
One real sync call for every single write, no more and no fewer.

lines.text: A well-known database's own documentation makes a specific claim about why keeping a write-ahead log helps at all.
What does it actually say gets to skip the flush?
Every other data file the transaction touched.
Only the log file itself needs flushing to guarantee the commit.
The documentation's own words: keeping a log means only that log needs flushing, not every file a transaction changed.
And under real load, one flush can cover many small transactions committing around the same moment.
None of this matters if the drive itself is lying about it.

lines.text: So, pulling this topic together: flushing after every write made a real call every single time, a thousand of them.
Batching into deliberate flush points cut that to twenty-one calls, and was dramatically faster for the identical writes.
A write-ahead log's own documentation explains why: one flush can cover many transactions at once.
And none of it is real durability until a forced flush makes a volatile write cache tell the truth.
